items.stem: A HIPAA-covered Massachusetts pharmacy discovers a reportable breach of unsecured PHI affecting 34 patients in October 2026. No exception or law-enforcement delay applies. Which federal reporting timetable is correct?

choices.text: Notify affected patients only with the next annual HIPAA report.
choices.why: Affected individuals have a prompt, no-later-than-60-day notification rule.

choices.text: Notify patients within 60 days; report to HHS by 60 days after year-end.
choices.why: HIPAA has separate individual and small-breach HHS reporting clocks.

choices.text: Notify both HHS and each patient only after the calendar year closes.
choices.why: The HHS under-500 schedule does not defer individual notice.

choices.text: HIPAA never applies when fewer than 500 people are affected.
choices.why: Small breaches still require notification.

items.stem: A covered pharmacy determines that a breach of unsecured PHI has affected 520 people. The risk assessment did not establish a low probability of compromise and no permitted delay applies. Which HHS notification standard governs?

choices.text: Only the next annual small-breach log.
choices.why: That option applies to fewer than 500 affected individuals.

choices.text: An open-ended deadline decided by the pharmacy's vendor.
choices.why: Business arrangements do not eliminate the regulated timing.

choices.text: Notice solely to Massachusetts police; HHS is never involved.
choices.why: A covered entity must follow the federal HHS breach-reporting rule.

choices.text: Notify HHS without unreasonable delay, within 60 calendar days.
choices.why: The at-least-500 category requires timely reporting to the HHS Secretary.

items.topic: HIPAA substitute notice for outdated addresses
items.stem: A HIPAA-covered pharmacy discovers a reportable breach of unsecured PHI involving 25 patients. Twelve affected patients have outdated mailing addresses and no current email addresses. What substitute notification route may be required for these hard-to-reach individuals?

choices.text: No notice is needed because their original mailing information is outdated.
choices.why: A lack of current contact information does not eliminate notification requirements.

choices.text: Use a 90-day website notice or major-media notice, with a toll-free contact number.
choices.why: HIPAA substitute notice rule provides these options when contact information is insufficient for ten or more people.

choices.text: Keep a confidential staff-only memo with no public notice.
choices.why: An internal memorandum does not reach affected individuals.

choices.text: Send the pharmacy's standard payment invoice to one representative of the group.
choices.why: A payment invoice to an unrelated person is not an authorized substitute notice.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy discovers that an unauthorized person obtained a file containing Massachusetts residents' personal information as defined under M.G.L. c.93H. A supervisor assumes the HIPAA 60-day outside limit authorizes waiting 60 days for ALL Massachusetts notices. Which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Massachusetts Chapter 93H notification duties have their own 'as soon as practicable and without unreasonable delay' standard.
choices.why: The state breach statute has its own timeliness rule.

choices.text: If HIPAA applies, complying with its outer deadline automatically satisfies every state's notice requirement.
choices.why: Federal and state notification clocks and covered data can differ.

choices.text: The organization must consider its written information security program and applicable state reporting duties.
choices.why: 201 CMR 17.00 requires a comprehensive WISP for qualifying personal information and state reporting rules apply.

choices.text: Massachusetts law exempts healthcare organizations from all WISP safeguards.
choices.why: Healthcare entities are not categorically exempt from the Massachusetts safeguards.

items.stem: Two Massachusetts retail pharmacies share prescription processing. A drug interaction alert was overridden remotely, and the software records only a generic 'completed' status with no user identity or time. Which improvement is required under Board shared-service policy?

choices.text: Log processing steps, the responsible people and the dates/times.
choices.why: Board Policy 2021-02 requires an audit trail including date/time and the individuals involved.

choices.text: Delete the remote event because the final pharmacist reviewed the label.
choices.why: Final review does not remove the audit-trail obligation.

choices.text: Share only a weekly total of all prescriptions without case detail.
choices.why: An aggregate volume report cannot trace a single questionable transaction.

choices.text: Allow anyone at either pharmacy to use the same generic login.
choices.why: An unaccountable shared login undermines required traceability and data integrity.

items.stem: Two independently owned Massachusetts pharmacies plan a remote processing relationship. They do not share an owner and have no written service agreement, but both use the same computer software. What does the Board policy require?

choices.text: Common software alone is a complete substitute for written responsibilities.
choices.why: Technical access does not satisfy the written agreement requirement for independent owners.

choices.text: Write a shared-service agreement assigning each pharmacy's duties and oversight.
choices.why: The policy allows shared service among different owners when a suitable written contract exists.

choices.text: Buy an additional DEA Form 222 for each remotely reviewed Schedule VI prescription.
choices.why: A Form 222 is a Schedule II order instrument, not a shared-service contract.

choices.text: Stop all processing even after a compliant written agreement exists.
choices.why: The policy permits qualifying shared services.

items.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy has operated under a valid written central-fill shared-service agreement for three years. Its staff review policies only when an adverse event occurs and have not documented an annual review. What must change?

choices.text: The written agreement automatically removes all policy review obligations once signed.
choices.why: Board shared-service policy requires ongoing compliance review of procedures.

choices.text: A biennial review is sufficient if both pharmacies have the same software.
choices.why: Use of shared software does not determine the required policy-review frequency.

choices.text: Review shared-service policies and procedures at least annually and document needed updates.
choices.why: Board Policy 2021-02 §III(n)–(o) requires participating pharmacies to maintain and review procedures.

choices.text: Only the remote pharmacy has documentation duties; the originating pharmacy is fully exempt.
choices.why: Participating pharmacies share defined responsibilities and required procedures.

items.stem: A Massachusetts originating pharmacy learns that its participating central-fill location had an electronic record outage and cannot produce a reliable patient-specific audit trail for a prepared medication. The originating store wants to release the package solely because its shipping label matches. What should occur?

choices.text: Release automatically because central-fill work is wholly the other store's responsibility.
choices.why: Participants are jointly accountable and patient safety may not be compromised.

choices.text: Erase the outage from the shared database to restore the planned transaction history.
choices.why: Deletion defeats secure record integrity and traceability.

choices.text: Hand the package to the courier without final validation.
choices.why: Final dispensing validation and applicable shared-service controls still apply.

choices.text: Hold release until the patient-specific record is verified and the responsible parties identified.
choices.why: The joint controls require a valid, auditable prescription process.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy dispenses a manufacturer's refrigerated injection that must remain at 2–8°C. An outsourced courier says temperature control only matters while the injection is physically inside the pharmacy. Which rule addresses the shipment?

choices.text: Maintain the required cold chain during transportation and delivery too.
choices.why: Board Policy 2020-05 §II explicitly applies cold-chain control to delivery and shipping.

choices.text: Move the injection to an ambient shipping bag once it leaves the building.
choices.why: The manufacturer's specified stability and the cold chain continue during transit.

choices.text: Change the package label to 'room temperature' without stability evidence.
choices.why: Relabeling cannot override storage specifications.

choices.text: Use the policy's freezer range for every refrigerator medication.
choices.why: Refrigeration and freezing are different storage conditions.

items.stem: The pharmacy's refrigerator has a valid temperature log and appropriate design. A planned electrical shutdown will interrupt power overnight, but no arrangement exists to preserve refrigerated drug stock elsewhere. Under Massachusetts Board Policy 2020-05, what is specifically missing?

choices.text: Maintain a backup plan protecting refrigerated medicines during power failures.
choices.why: The policy requires a backup plan for power failure or other unforeseen event.

choices.text: Another thermometer reading from the last normal workday.
choices.why: A historical normal reading does not replace a power outage backup plan.

choices.text: A DEA Schedule II perpetual record entry for every vaccine in the refrigerator.
choices.why: Refrigeration continuity does not automatically make noncontrolled vaccines Schedule II substances.

choices.text: A manufacturer's automatic authorization to extend every drug's expiry by 30 days.
choices.why: An outage does not automatically justify any product's extended dating.

items.stem: A pharmacy receives returned refrigerated medication with verified temperature excursion beyond its labeled storage range. A technician suggests adjusting the expiration date by one day and placing it back on saleable stock. What is the best response?

choices.text: Release because it is still before the manufacturer's printed expiration date.
choices.why: An expiration date presumes compliant storage; excursion must be assessed.

choices.text: Quarantine, evaluate stability evidence and document the decision before release.
choices.why: The storage and cold-chain obligations require a defensible integrity assessment, not an arbitrary relabel.

choices.text: Replace the temperature logger but keep the product without review.
choices.why: Changing monitoring equipment cannot establish suitability of exposed drug.

choices.text: Assume every excursion necessarily makes a product safe at 24 hours.
choices.why: Stability impact depends on the preparation and exposure.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy monitors vaccines with a digital refrigerator probe. The probe displays appropriate temperatures, but the pharmacy has no laboratory calibration-testing certificate and never follows the manufacturer's recommended recalibration schedule. What policy-specific corrective action is required?

choices.text: Treat the display's precision as proof of accuracy without external calibration.
choices.why: A displayed decimal does not replace the policy's calibration-certificate requirement.

choices.text: Use a certified calibrated thermometer and follow its recalibration schedule.
choices.why: Board Policy 2020-05 §VII requires a documented calibration-testing certificate from an accredited laboratory.

choices.text: Measure temperature only when a vaccine shipment is unpacked.
choices.why: The policy also requires routine monitoring and review of every cold-storage unit.

choices.text: Use a household kitchen thermometer in place of a certified temperature probe.
choices.why: An uncertified consumer thermometer is not an equivalent documented control.

items.stem: A pharmacy delivers filled prescriptions to an employer's designated worksite collection desk under a compliant Massachusetts worksite program. The collecting employee leaves early, and the pharmacy delivery agent proposes leaving undelivered medication in the worksite office overnight. What should happen?

choices.text: Leave the medication in a locked worksite drawer for pickup tomorrow regardless of the pharmacy's agreement.
choices.why: The worksite collection rule does not permit routine overnight storage of undelivered prescriptions at the site.

choices.text: Give the undelivered items to an unlicensed coworker who recognizes the patient's name.
choices.why: Recognizing a name is not sufficient for a lawful handoff.

choices.text: Return undelivered prescriptions to the pharmacy through its authorized collection/delivery process.
choices.why: 247 CMR 9.04(9) requires undelivered medications to return to pharmacy custody.

choices.text: Record the drugs as administered at the worksite so the chain of custody is complete.
choices.why: Dispensing and administration are different events; documentation cannot invent an administration.

items.stem: A pharmacy begins a home-delivery program for Schedule III and Schedule VI prescriptions. The manager argues that FDA labeling and the courier's standard service agreement replace any pharmacy written procedure. What remains specifically required?

choices.text: No written policy because couriers own the delivery vehicle.
choices.why: Pharmacy responsibility is not discharged by using a courier.

choices.text: Maintain written policies for controlled-drug delivery, packaging and transport.
choices.why: 247 CMR 9.02(3) specifically requires these pharmacy controls.

choices.text: One universal DEA Form 222 for every Schedule III and Schedule VI package.
choices.why: Form 222 is for registrant ordering of Schedule I–II, not patient delivery of these products.

choices.text: A patient must travel to the pharmacy to sign all delivery records in person.
choices.why: The law does not categorically prohibit authorized home delivery.

items.stem: During the same delivery route, a courier leaves a refrigerated injection at a locked door without confirmation and sends another patient's medicine to the wrong address. Which separate pharmacy risks need to be assessed? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Temperature exposure, drug stability, and chain-of-custody for the unattended injection.
choices.why: Delivery cannot be judged only by possession of a shipping tracking number.

choices.text: Confidentiality, recipient identity, and whether the other patient's medicine can safely be recovered or replaced.
choices.why: Wrong-recipient delivery raises privacy and product integrity issues.

choices.text: Both products may automatically be returned to saleable stock when the courier retrieves the boxes.
choices.why: The products must be assessed for delivery status and integrity before any disposition.

choices.text: Documentation, incident response and whether any applicable breach notification standard is triggered.
choices.why: Proper response requires determining the facts and applicable reporting standards, rather than assuming none apply.

items.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy operates a lawful workplace prescription delivery and collection program. A company employee asks to obtain a prescription for a friend who does not work at the company and does not live with the employee. No other lawful patient agent authorization exists. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.text: The worksite program's special collection service does not extend to this unrelated friend.
choices.why: 247 CMR 9.04(9) limits qualifying worksite recipients; separate proper patient-agent authorization would need review.

choices.text: All friends of any employee are covered whenever the courier arrives at the workplace.
choices.why: The special workplace collection rule has defined eligible people.

choices.text: The pharmacy may transfer any other person's prescription into the program without checking the actual recipient.
choices.why: A service contract does not waive recipient eligibility and dispensing safeguards.

choices.text: Only Schedule II medications may be delivered in a worksite program.
choices.why: The provision is not a Schedule II-only collection rule.

items.stem: An overnight network outage requires a Massachusetts pharmacy to process urgent, otherwise valid prescriptions through its contingency workflow. The computer returns the next morning, but the manager wants to discard all paper records without updating the electronic patient profiles. What is required?

choices.text: Discard all downtime records once the computers reboot.
choices.why: A downtime process must reconcile dispensed medication into the electronic records.

choices.text: Back-enter downtime prescriptions and document the appropriate DUR.
choices.why: 247 CMR 9.19(22) includes continuity, record reconciliation and DUR procedures.

choices.text: Stop all pharmacist clinical review for the entire outage.
choices.why: The downtime policy must include an appropriate drug utilization review.

choices.text: Recreate the dispensing labels from memory and omit the date of each supply.
choices.why: Record integrity requires accurate entries rather than undocumented reconstruction.

items.stem: A pharmacy completes a major renovation and appoints a new Manager of Record in the same week. The owner proposes doing the next Board self-inspection at the annual renewal six months later. Which statements apply? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Conduct an applicable self-inspection within seven days of the renovation or MOR change.

choices.text: Annual inspection alone always replaces event-triggered inspection.
choices.why: An annual minimum does not waive the seven-day event requirement.

choices.text: Use a Board-approved inspection tool appropriate to the pharmacy's operations.
choices.why: The rule specifies applicable routine and compounding tools.

choices.text: Retain the completed self-inspection tool for at least two years.
choices.why: 247 CMR 9.19(21) includes the retention period.

items.stem: The last pharmacist locks a Massachusetts retail pharmacy that is inside a supermarket. Management plans to switch off the pharmacy alarm because the outer supermarket is still open. What does 247 CMR 9.21 require?

choices.text: Turn off the pharmacy alarm because the store has customer service staff.
choices.why: The pharmacy must activate its own security system when closed.

choices.text: Leave the secured prescription area unlocked for cleaning staff.
choices.why: Access and physical pharmacy security must remain controlled.

choices.text: Keep the pharmacy prescription area separately locked and alarmed when closed.
choices.why: 247 CMR 9.21(3),(5) requires an activated alarm and separate secured area.

choices.text: Only protect Schedule II inventory; all other pharmacy controls may be unlocked.
choices.why: Pharmacy controlled substances and secure prescription areas have broader requirements.

items.stem: After flooding disables a Massachusetts pharmacy computer, a delivery includes an unreconciled Schedule II shipment and a refrigerated product that exceeded its labeled temperature range. The pharmacy is open under its downtime policy. Which plan best meets the distinct responsibilities?

choices.text: Dispense everything once the courier signs a delivery ticket.
choices.why: A delivery signature does not resolve inventory discrepancies or medication stability.

choices.text: Hold all future dispensing indefinitely with no continuity procedure.
choices.why: A pharmacy downtime policy must address appropriate lawful filling and continuity of care.

choices.text: Change the temperature log and reset the controlled-stock balance without investigation.
choices.why: Falsifying records and bypassing reconciliation are inconsistent with record and security duties.

choices.text: Quarantine stock, reconcile Schedule II inventory and use downtime controls for safe dispensing.
choices.why: The combined regulations require separate inventory, storage-integrity and continuity-of-care controls.
